name: Bran
lede: Bran is a warm tan, the brown of wheat bran, and a name the books mention more as a dye-vat ingredient than as a color.

sections.title: The color and the name
sections.body: Paterson defines bran simply as the brown color of bran, filed among the browns [1]. Maerz and Paul (1930) record the name from 1925, on plate 12 D 7 [2]. No book we hold says who first used it as a color word, which is undocumented here [1][2].

sections.title: Bran in the dye vat
sections.body:
Where the books talk about bran, it is a dyer's material. In Balfour-Paul's account of medieval woad-vat recipes studied by Cardon, a vat on the verge of going off could be rescued with hot madder dye or bran [3]. For imported indigo, European dyers made a "madder soup" from bran, [[irresistible]] and burnt lees [3]. Japanese indigo dyers add rice bran, rice wine, honey or lime to speed a slow fermentation [3].

One English recipe for the fastest dark blue, quoted by Garfield, uses a peck of bran, the refuse of wheat, with woad, madder, copperas and lime [4]. Bran also served as a swindler's filler: in the mid-nineteenth century Salter recorded commercial madder root adulterated with brickdust, ochre, sand and bran [5]. None of this says the dye looked like bran. The shared word is a kitchen word.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of color distance, in 3,156 paintings, or 13 per cent, one of the most common colors in the archive [6]. As photographed, it often reflects aged paper and silk as much as paint [6].

It is strongest in the 1300s, at 85 of 251 paintings, two and a half times the archive rate [6]. Mughal painting carries it in 90 of 168 works, four times the rate [6]. The top match is the Chinese hanging scroll *White-Robed Guanyin* of about 1250, where it fills 92 per cent of the work [6]. Nearest company: [[camel]], [[sienna]] and [[ochre]] [6].
